 Before You Vote: A Practical Breakdown for Indiana’s 2026 Midterms 
McKenzie Conrad
 Senior Communications Specialist 
 she/her/hers 
 October 23, 2026 
 Student ID restrictions, voter registration purges, and more: what’s new and what remains the same for the 2026 election. 
 The vote is precious. It is almost sacred. It’s the most powerful non-violent tool we have in a democratic society.
 — John Lewis, 2013 
 We are closing in on a midterm election during an unprecedented year. We’ve seen communities push back against a morally bankrupt and deadly immigration enforcement scheme, with Indiana being a testing ground for harmful anti-immigrant laws and detention practices. Investigations have been waged against journalists and political opponents, and a movement to restrict and reverse voting protections have dominated the news cycle for months. In short: the civic responsibility and significance of your vote, particularly here in Indiana, can’t be overstated.
 With the constant firehose of news, it’s hard to cut through the headlines to find what actually impacts us as voters and the facts we need to know.
 What’s Changed for Indiana Voters Since 2024? 
 SEA 10 (2025) : This is an important change: it bans the use of college and university IDs as a valid form of voter identification in Indiana. Although it was temporarily blocked by a federal judge in April, an appeals court allowed it to remain in effect while the case continues.
 Students can no longer use their college IDs at the polls.  By June, the state had cancelled 981 existing voter registrations and rejected 644 new applications . Outdated BMV records can flag people who have since become U.S. citizens, putting eligible voters at risk of losing their right to vote.  What’s Hasn’t Changed: A Fact Check 
 There’s lots of confusion and talk about federal election rules, including the president’s efforts to restrict mail-in voting. But the president cannot change election laws on his own. States run elections under state and federal law , and executive orders can be challenged in court.
 You can still vote by mail – nothing’s changed! Indiana still allows absentee voting if you need the requirements (e.g., 65 and older, people with disabilities, or those away on Election Day).
 You can still vote early…now! In-person early voting started October 6, and you don’t need a special reason to do it.
 Indiana’s early voting window remains the same. A bill was introduced in 2026 attempting to cut early voting in half, but it was rejected, meaning early voting is still 28 days.
 You don’t need new documents to vote. Despite proposals to require proof of citizenship, Indiana’s regular voter ID rules still apply at the polls. You do not need to bring a birth certificate or other citizenship paperwork just to cast your ballot.
 You can still vote on Election Day. Polls will be open Tuesday, November 3, from 6 a.m. to 6 p.m. local time.
 With talk of federal agents at polling places, remember that no one, including federal immigration agents, can legally threaten, intimidate, or prevent you from voting.  If you have any questions about your rights before, during, or after voting, call the Election Protection Hotline at 866-OUR-VOTE (866-687-8683). 
 Also, remember. Don’t spread misinformation about intimidation at the polls. You should only share information that is accurate and comes from reliable sources.
 What Should I Expect on My Ballot? 
 Federal Lawmakers 
 U.S. House of Representatives: All nine Indiana seats are up for election. Members of Congress write federal laws, vote on spending, and help oversee federal agencies.
 State Lawmakers 
 Indiana House of Representatives: All 100 seats are up for election. They vote on state laws and budgets affecting everything from public schools to health care and civil rights.
 Indiana Senate: Half of the 50 seats are up for election. Senators work with the Indiana House to pass state laws and approve the state budget.
 State Offices 
 Secretary of State: Oversees elections and voter registration systems, regulates certain state financial areas, and manages business registrations in Indiana.
 State Treasurer: Manages and invests Indiana’s money and oversees financial programs, including college savings accounts.
 State Comptroller: Tracks how state money is spent, pays state bills and employees, and distributes tax revenue to local governments and schools.
 Local Elections 
 Depending on where you live, you may also see:
 Sheriff: Oversees county law enforcement and the county jail.
 Prosecutor: Determines what criminal charges to pursue and represents the state in criminal cases.
 County Council and Commissioners: Make decisions about local budgets, spending, county services, and infrastructure.
 School Board: Makes decisions about school policies, budgets, curriculum, and district leadership.
 Township Trustee: Provides certain emergency assistance to residents and may oversee local fire protection services.
 Judges and Public Questions 
 Judicial Retention: Some judges will appear on your ballot without an opponent. Instead, you’ll vote YES or NO on whether they should keep their jobs for another term. Depending on where you live, you may also see judges running in contested elections.
 Public Question 1 (Right to Bail): Would expand when judges can deny bail to people accused of crimes, even before they’ve been convicted. A YES vote would expand that authority, while a NO vote would keep the current constitutional protections in place. Learn more here .
 Public Question 2 (Judges’ Residency): Would change where city and town court judges are allowed to live, letting them reside in the county where their court is located or an adjoining county instead of the city/town. A YES vote would allow this change, while a NO vote would keep the current residency requirements.
 Before You Head to the Polls 
 It’s important to note again that your ballot depends on where you live. Visit IndianaVoters.in.gov to find your sample ballot, see who’s running, and research your choices before voting!
 Keep the following election dates handy, as well:
 October 6: Early voting opened
 October 22: Deadline to apply for an absentee ballot
 November 2: In-person early voting ends at noon
 November 3: Election Day (6 a.m. to 6 p.m.)
 Check your polling location, ensure you work out arrangements for transportation, work, and childcare. \n","image_video_field_group":{"image_video_options":"image","image_group":{"image":false,"caption":"","credit":"","link-settings":"none","url":""},"video_group":{"video":false,"cover_image":false,"video_orientation":"standard"},"youtube_group":{"oembed-url":"","cover-image":false}}},{"title":"Leave political merch at home.
